lead: A stringer or frame made of thin flat walls can fail in compression without bending as a whole. Its widest flat element buckles first, at a stress set by its width-to-thickness ratio b/t, and the section then keeps carrying load through its corners until the corners yield and the whole section folds. That final load is the crippling load, and the average stress at it is the crippling stress σ<sub>cs</sub>. Needham's and Gerard's methods estimate σ<sub>cs</sub> from b/t and the material, and the rivets that join stringer to skin bring two more local checks: inter-rivet buckling and wrinkling.
prereq: You need: the plate buckling stress and the buckling coefficients for different edge supports from buckling of thin plates.

blocks.text: A thin-walled section such as an angle, channel, Z or hat is a composite shape: a set of flat plate elements joined along their edges. Each element in compression is a long plate. A web between two flanges has both long edges supported; an outstanding flange has one supported and one free. Its elastic local buckling stress is:

blocks.where: σ<sub>el</sub> is the local buckling stress (N/mm²); k = 4.0 for an element with both long edges simply supported and k = 0.425 for one with a free edge; b the flat width of the element (mm); t its thickness (mm).

blocks.text: Choose k for the edge condition first. The elements of a section buckle together, because they share their edges: the weakest element tries to buckle first and is partly held by its stiffer neighbours, so the section local buckling stress lies between the values for its elements taken alone.

Local buckling does not end the strength of the section. The corners, where two elements meet, cannot buckle and keep taking load after the flat parts have buckled. Load rises until the material at the corners yields; then the section folds locally. This is crippling, and the crippling stress σ<sub>cs</sub> = P<sub>cs</sub>/A is the average stress over the whole section at that load. It is above σ<sub>el</sub> for thin sections and cannot exceed the compressive yield stress σ<sub>cy</sub>.

sections.h3: Crippling stress by Needham's and Gerard's methods

blocks.text: Both methods fit tests on short lengths of formed and extruded sections. Needham cut each section into angles and found that an angle's crippling stress depends on its legs through b′/t:

blocks.where: σ<sub>cs</sub> is the crippling stress of the angle (N/mm²); σ<sub>cy</sub> the compressive yield stress (N/mm²); E Young's modulus (N/mm²); a and b the leg lengths (mm); t the thickness (mm); C<sub>e</sub> = 0.316 when both leg edges are free, 0.342 when one is free and 0.366 when neither is free.

blocks.text: A channel, Z or hat is cut into angles at the middle of its webs. A cut edge is not free, because the rest of the section holds it, so a channel becomes two angles each with one free edge. Each angle is given its crippling load σ<sub>cs</sub> A, and the section crippling stress is the total load over the total area, σ<sub>cs</sub> = ΣP/ΣA.
Gerard correlated the same kind of tests with a single parameter that counts how many flat elements the section has for its area. For angles, tubes, multi-corner sections and stiffened plates:

blocks.where: A is the section area (mm²); g is the number of flanges plus the number of cuts needed to divide the section into angles; the other symbols as above.

blocks.text: For two-corner sections (Z, J and channel) Gerard gives a separate formula of the same kind with its own constants, taken from the data sheet used in the course. Both methods must be capped: σ<sub>cs</sub> is never taken above σ<sub>cy</sub>, and data sheets set lower caps for some shapes.

sections.h3: Inter-rivet buckling, wrinkling and the design checks

blocks.text: A skin riveted to a stringer is pinned to it only at the rivets. Between two rivets at pitch s the skin is a short, wide strip in compression that can bow away from the stringer like a column with partly fixed ends. Treating it as a plate strip of length s:

blocks.where: σ<sub>ir</sub> is the inter-rivet buckling stress (N/mm²); s the rivet pitch along the load (mm); t the skin thickness (mm); c the end fixity, 4 for fully fixed ends and 1 for pinned ends; flush rivets give less fixity than protruding heads.

blocks.text: If σ<sub>ir</sub> is below the stringer stress, the skin bows away between rivets and the panel loses its effective skin; close the pitch or thicken the skin. Wrinkling is a different local failure: in a skin on a stringer flange, the skin and the attached flange buckle together in short waves at the attachment line, and the flange is pulled or pushed out of plane. It depends on skin thickness, flange thickness, rivet size and spacing, and is checked from test-based charts; it can set a lower stress than the crippling of the stringer.

figure.caption: Crippling stress of an equal angle against b′/t for the worked example's alloy. Needham's curve (C<sub>e</sub> = 0.316) and Gerard's (g = 2) both fall as b′/t rises and are cut off at σ<sub>cy</sub> = 300 MPa. At the example's b′/t = 20 they give 155 and 135 MPa, about twice the 70.6 MPa at which each leg buckles locally (dashed).

spec.aria: A graph of stress from 0 to 350 megapascals against b prime over t from 5 to 40. A horizontal dashed line at 300 marks the yield cut-off. Two falling curves, Needham and Gerard, start at the cut-off for stocky angles and fall as the ratio grows; a steeper dashed curve shows elastic local buckling of a leg. At b prime over t of 20 the points read Needham 155, Gerard 135 and local buckling 70.6 megapascals. Beside the graph a sketch of the 30 by 30 by 1.5 millimetre angle.

examples.question: An extruded equal angle has legs of 30 mm and is 1.5 mm thick. The alloy has E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33 and σ<sub>cy</sub> = 300 MPa. Find the local buckling stress of one leg, and the crippling stress and load by Needham's and by Gerard's method.
steps: Needham: b′ = (30 + 30)/2 = 30 mm, b′/t = 20; both leg edges are free, so C<sub>e</sub> = 0.316. √(σ<sub>cy</sub> E) = √(300 × 72,000) = 4,647.6 MPa.
Gerard: an angle has two flanges and needs no cut, so g = 2. g t²/A = 2 × 2.25/90 = 0.050; √(E/σ<sub>cy</sub>) = √240 = 15.49; product 0.7746.

Checks: both are below σ<sub>cy</sub> = 300 MPa, so no cap is needed, and both are about twice σ<sub>el</sub>: the corner carries load long after the legs buckle. The methods differ by 15%; take the lower for design.
examples.answer: σ<sub>el</sub> = 70.6 MPa; Needham σ<sub>cs</sub> = 155 MPa (P<sub>cs</sub> = 14.0 kN); Gerard σ<sub>cs</sub> = 135 MPa (P<sub>cs</sub> = 12.2 kN).

examples.question: A formed channel has a 60 mm web and two 25 mm flanges, all 1.5 mm thick, in the same alloy (E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33, σ<sub>cy</sub> = 300 MPa). Find the local buckling stresses of the web and flanges and the crippling load by Needham's method.
steps: Web, both edges supported (k = 4): σ<sub>el</sub> = 4 × 66,455 × (1.5/60)² = 166.1 MPa. Flange, one free edge (k = 0.425): σ<sub>el</sub> = 0.425 × 66,455 × (1.5/25)² = 101.7 MPa. The flanges buckle first.
Cut the web at mid-depth: two angles, each with a 25 mm flange (free edge) and a 30 mm half-web (cut edge, held by the other half). One edge free, so C<sub>e</sub> = 0.342.
Area: each angle (25 + 30) × 1.5 = 82.5 mm², the section 165 mm².
examples.answer: σ<sub>el</sub> = 166.1 MPa (web) and 101.7 MPa (flanges); σ<sub>cs</sub> = 179 MPa and P<sub>cs</sub> = 29.6 kN.

traps: Using k = 4 for an outstanding flange. A flange with one free edge has k = 0.425; k = 4 makes it nearly ten times too strong.
Taking the local buckling stress σ<sub>el</sub> as the failure stress. The section cripples later, when the corners yield.
Calling a cut edge free in Needham's method. A web cut at mid-depth is held by the rest of the section; only true outstanding edges are free.
Using the panel width or stringer pitch for inter-rivet buckling. The length is the rivet pitch s along the load.

quiz.q: Define the crippling stress of a thin-walled section.
quiz.a: The average compressive stress over the whole section, P<sub>cs</sub>/A, at which the section fails by local folding after its flat elements have buckled and its corners have yielded.

quiz.q: Write Needham's formula and give C<sub>e</sub> for an angle with both edges free.
quiz.a: σ<sub>cs</sub>/√(σ<sub>cy</sub> E) = C<sub>e</sub>/(b′/t)<sup>0.75</sup> with b′ = (a + b)/2; C<sub>e</sub> = 0.316.

quiz.q: Why is σ<sub>cs</sub> of a thin section well above the local buckling stress of its flat elements?
quiz.a: The flat elements buckle, but the corners where they meet cannot. The corners keep taking load, as the sheet next to a stringer does, until the material there yields. Only then does the section fold.

quiz.q: A 1.2 mm skin is riveted to stringers at a pitch of 25 mm (E = 72 GPa, ν = 0.33). Find the inter-rivet buckling stress for c = 4 and c = 1, and the largest pitch with c = 4 if the stringer works at 150 MPa.
quiz.a: π²E/[12(1 − ν²)] = 66,455 MPa; (t/s)² = 0.00230. c = 4: σ<sub>ir</sub> = 612 MPa (an elastic value above yield, so yield would govern); c = 1: 153 MPa. For 150 MPa with c = 4: s = t √(4 × 66,455/150) = 50.5 mm. Even with pinned ends σ<sub>ir</sub> = 153 MPa just exceeds 150 MPa, so the 25 mm pitch is safe; with full fixity it could be about doubled.

Inter-rivet buckling is the skin bowing away from the stringer between two rivets, a column-like failure set by t/s and the rivet fixity. Wrinkling is the skin and stringer flange buckling together in short waves at the attachment line, set by the skin and flange thicknesses and the rivet size and spacing, and checked from test charts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry keeps crippling allowables as test databases. Search for crippling stress, Gerard method and inter-rivet buckling.
